title: Advisory Opinion 26-03: Security Grant to Legislators
text:
State of Colorado
Daniel Wolf, Chair Independent Ethics Commission
Cyril Vidergar, Vice-Chair 1300 Broadway, Suite 240
Lori Laske, Commissioner Denver CO 80203
Andrew Lillie, Commissioner Phone: (303) 223-0110
Sarah Mercer, Commissioner iec.colorado.gov
Dino Ioannides, Executive Director
Advisory Opinion 26-031
(Security Grant to Legislators)
Summary: Under the facts and circumstances of this request, it would not violate Section 3 of
the Colorado Constitution, Article XXIX, or Section 24-18-104(1), C.R.S., for the General
Assembly to accept a security grant from the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Further, it would not violate Section 3 of the Colorado Constitution, Article XXIX, or Section
24-18-104(1), for individual legislators to accept reimbursement for security purchases, where
the reimbursement is available equally to all Colorado state legislators, the funds will assist the
legislators in their legislative duties, and no additional ethical concerns exist.
I. Jurisdiction
Requestor is a member of the Colorado Legislative Council Staff, seeking an advisory opinion2
on behalf of the Colorado General Assembly (the “Legislature”). Both the Requestor, as a
government employee, and members of the Legislature (“legislators”) are subject to IEC
jurisdiction under Article XXIX of the Colorado Constitution.
1 This Advisory Opinion was originally docketed, and appeared on the Commission’s agenda of
May 19, 2026, as Letter Ruling 26-01. For reasons described in footnote 2, this opinion is
renumbered as Advisory Opinion 26-03.
2 Requestor sought a “Letter Ruling.” However, the letter ruling statute states, “Any person who
is not a . . . government employee may submit a request to the commission for a letter ruling[.]”
§24-18.5-101(4)(b)(III), C.R.S. (emphasis added). As Requestor is on the Legislative Council
Staff, she is a “government employee” and cannot seek a letter ruling.
However, the advisory opinion provision from the Colorado Constitution states that a
“government employee may submit a written request to the independent ethics commission for
an advisory opinion on whether any conduct by that person would constitute a violation of”
applicable ethics provisions. Colo. Const. art. XXIX, § 5(5). Although Requestor would not be
in violation of ethics provisions herself, as she is administering this grant rather than receiving a
gift, it is arguable that her “conduct” could cause—and thus constitute—a violation by causing
legislators to accept improper gifts. So, this request will be treated as one for an advisory
opinion.
1

Any person subject to IEC jurisdiction may submit an advisory opinion request concerning
whether any conduct by that person would violate Article XXIX or any other standards of
conduct or reporting requirements as provided by law. Colo. Const. art. XXIX, § 5(5).
The Commission considers such requests pursuant to IEC Rule 3.
II. Factual Background
Colorado pays over $230,000 per year in membership dues to the National Conference of State
Legislatures (“NCSL”). NCSL has a security fund to help address threats to state legislators’
safety, particularly when away from the Capitol. NCSL has indicated that the Colorado General
Assembly is eligible for a grant up to $20,000.
The grant would be awarded to Colorado’s Legislative Department Cash Fund (the “Fund”),
which is authorized to receive gifts, grants, and donations. The Fund is appropriated to the
Executive Committee of the Legislative Council to pay for Legislative Department expenses. If
NCSL approves Colorado’s grant application, it may award the grant upfront. In order for NCSL
to approve the application, Colorado must:
• Certify that any applicable ethics laws and provisions are satisfied;
• Make the program available on a nonpartisan basis to all legislators in the applicant
chamber or legislature;
• Inform legislators that funding for the programs and services is provided through the
NCSL Legislator Security Fund;
• Ensure that legislators’ personal expenses to be reimbursed meet the eligibility criteria as
outlined in the funding notice; and
• Certify that legislative leadership approves the application.
If approved, each legislator would be eligible for reimbursement up to $2003 for personal
security expenses between the policy’s issuance and October 15, 2026. Eligible expenses
include:
• fees for home security monitoring services;
• subscription fees for identity monitoring or personal information protection services for
the legislator (e.g., DeleteMe);
• fees for the legislator to attend personal security or self-defense classes; and
3 There are one hundred Colorado legislators between the House and Senate, so each legislator
would be eligible for this program ($200 x 100 = $20,000).
2

• the purchase of security system equipment, including cameras, video doorbells, and alarm
systems for a legislator’s personal home, to be returned to the General Assembly upon
conclusion of a member’s term of office.
The following expenses are ineligible:
• purchase of equipment that will be retained by a legislator after their term of office ends;
and
• services purchased prior to the effective date of the policy or after October 15, 2026.
To receive reimbursement, a legislator needs to purchase the equipment or service, provide an
itemized receipt, and agree in writing to abide by the above requirements. After October 15,
2026, any unused funds will be returned to NCSL.
The Requestor oversees the Legislative Council Staff that will administer the grants.
III. Applicable Law
The Colorado Constitution, Article XXIX, Section 3 (gift ban) prohibits certain gifts to public
officers:
(2) No public officer, member of the general assembly, local government official,
or government employee, either directly or indirectly as the beneficiary of a gift or
thing of value given to such person’s spouse or dependent child, shall solicit, accept
or receive any gift or other thing of value having either a fair market value or
aggregate actual cost greater than fifty dollars ($50) [now $75] in any calendar year,
including but not limited to, gifts, loans, travel, entertainment, or special discounts,
from a person, without the person receiving lawful consideration of equal or greater
value in return from the public officer, member of the general assembly, local
government official, or government employee who solicited, accepted or received
the gift or other thing of value.
Section 3(3) includes exceptions to the gift ban, one of which is if the “gift or thing of value is
. . . [a] component of the compensation paid or other incentive given to the recipient in the
normal course of employment.” Colo. Const. art. XXIX, § 3(3)(h).
Section 3(2) does not prohibit gifts to a government entity, department, agency, or institution that
employs covered individuals.
In interpreting constitutional provisions, the IEC strives to “ascertain and give effect to the intent
of the electorate adopting the amendment.” Bolt v. Arapahoe County Sch. Dist. No. Six, 898
P.2d 525, 532 (Colo. 1995). If voters’ intent is unclear from the plain language, the IEC
construes the language in light of the objective sought to be achieved and the “mischief to be
avoided by the amendment.” Zaner v. City of Brighton, 917 P.2d 280, 283 (Colo. 1996). Where,
as here, the amendment was voter-initiated, the IEC adopts “an interpretation which harmonizes
different constitutional provisions rather than an interpretation which would create a conflict
3

between such provisions.” Id. at 283. The IEC rejects a “narrow or technical reading of the
language contained in the initiated constitutional amendment, if to do so would defeat the intent
of the people.” Id. Further, the IEC avoids any interpretation that would be an “absurd result.”
In re Interrogatories on House Bill 99-1325, 979 P.2d 549, 557 (Colo. 1999).
Colorado statutes also contain a gift ban:
A public officer, a member of the general assembly, a local government official, or
an employee shall not:
* * *
(b) Accept a gift of substantial value or a substantial economic benefit tantamount
to a gift of substantial value:
(I) Which would tend improperly to influence a reasonable person in his position
to depart from the faithful and impartial discharge of his public duties; or
(II) Which he knows or which a reasonable person in his position should know
under the circumstances is primarily for the purpose of rewarding him for official
action he has taken.
§ 24-18-104(1), C.R.S.
In interpreting and applying Section 24-18-104(1), the Commission must “discern and effectuate
the General Assembly’s intent . . . [by] apply[ing] words and phrases in accordance with their
plain and ordinary meanings[.]” Miller v. Crested Butte, LLC, 2024 CO 30, ¶ 23 (internal
citations omitted). Statutes must also be interpreted by looking “to the entire statutory scheme to
give consistent, harmonious, and sensible effect to all of its parts . . . [and to] avoid constructions
that would render any words or phrases superfluous or that would lead to illogical or absurd
results.” Id. When “construing a statute, we must respect the General Assembly’s choice of
language . . . [and] not add words to a statute or subtract words from it.” Id.
IV. Discussion
Requestor presents two inquiries: (1) whether it would violate ethics laws for the Legislature to
accept the grant from NCSL; and (2) whether it would violate ethics laws for the individual
legislators to accept reimbursement from the Legislature’s Fund for security purchases.
Regarding the first inquiry, the grant from NCSL to the Legislature’s Fund is unquestionably a
gift to a government entity, thus the Commission lacks jurisdiction over that issue and it would
not violate ethics laws.
Regarding the second inquiry, reimbursement for security purchases would also not violate
ethics laws. As this security funding is available equally to all Colorado state legislators, the
funds will assist the legislators in their legislative duties, and no additional ethical concerns exist,
the funding constitutes “[a] component of the compensation paid or other incentive given to the
recipient in the normal course of employment.” Colo. Const. art. XXIX, § 3(3)(h).
4

V. Conclusion
Under the facts and circumstances of this request, it would not violate Section 3 of the Colorado
Constitution, Article XXIX, or Section 24-18-104(1), C.R.S., for the Legislature to accept the
NCSL grant.
Further, it would not violate Section 3 of the Colorado Constitution, Article XXIX, or Section
24-18-104(1), C.R.S., for individual legislators to accept reimbursement for security purchases.
The IEC cautions that this opinion is based on the specific facts presented herein, and that
different facts could produce a different result. The IEC encourages individuals with particular
questions to request more fact-specific advice through requests for advisory opinions and letter
rulings related to their individual circumstances.
The Independent Ethics Commission
